digest.intro: Infrastructure under attack, weapons in orbit, and a bird frame from Bergen.

items.title: Coordinated rail sabotage hits the Netherlands on budget day
items.blurb: On Prinsjesdag — the Dutch equivalent of a State of the Union — pipes and cables were placed on tracks at 30+ locations simultaneously, shutting down routes to Schiphol, Utrecht, and Eindhoven. No suspects, no claimed motive; the AIVD (intelligence service) is now involved alongside police. Paired with a French train derailment the same week, the pattern is too tidy to be coincidence.

items.title: Trump, the Good Friday Agreement, Zelensky's refineries, and two chokepoints at once
items.blurb: De Arístegui's weekly dispatch is dense but earns it: Trump improvised Irish reunification comments and told Zelensky to stop hitting Russian fuel infrastructure — both from a golf resort terrace. The bigger story is buried underneath: Houthi forces have now taken Yemen's entire Red Sea coastline including Perim Island, which sits at the mouth of the Bab el-Mandeb, meaning both Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb face active simultaneous threat for the first time since WWII. A Russian drone also struck the locomotive of a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train minutes after an EU diplomatic convoy departed the same station.

items.title: The US military confirms it has weapons in orbit
items.blurb: Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said publicly, for the first time, that the US has placed "space control weapons" in orbit — no details on what they are or where, but the disclosure itself is the threshold event. This ends decades of studied ambiguity on US orbital weapons and will recalibrate every space-faring nation's posture, particularly China and Russia, who have been openly developing anti-satellite capabilities while the US officially denied having anything comparable.

items.title: 25 years of mass surveillance: a serious accounting
items.blurb: Schneier and Cindy Cohn use the 9/11 anniversary to trace how the legal architecture built for counterterrorism became a routine tool for ICE immigration enforcement and protest monitoring — and how it flows almost entirely through private companies (Google, Facebook, Flock, telecoms) rather than direct government collection. The argument isn't that it failed to stop attacks; it's that it succeeded at becoming infrastructure for something much broader and far less scrutinized than its original justification.

items.title: One cop, 19,000 cameras, reason given: 'LMAO'
items.blurb: An EFF analysis of Flock Safety's search logs found an officer in Lake County, Indiana searched license plates across 19,000 cameras covering 1,558 cities in a single query — logging the reason as 'LMAO.' Across dozens of agencies, audit logs showed 'idk', 'hehe', 'asdfg', and 6,300+ searches logged as 'TBD.' This is what Schneier's abstract argument looks like at the level of a Tuesday afternoon.

items.title: A bird frame that hears, identifies, and draws in 1800s naturalist style
items.blurb: A Raspberry Pi listens to the garden via mic, runs BirdNET-Go locally to identify species, then pulls from a hand-curated library of 800+ public-domain natural history illustrations — cut from real plates, not generated — and redraws an e-ink panel only when the birds actually change. The live version is running right now from a kitchen window in Bergen, Norway, showing whatever is in the garden at this moment. The 19th-century illustration constraint is the right aesthetic choice: it makes the technology disappear into something that feels like it always existed.

items.title: Andrew Thomas Huang on imperfection, puppetry, and resisting AI's psychic assault
items.blurb: Huang — who made the handmade surrealist films for Björk, FKA Twigs, and Thom Yorke — talks about why he keeps returning to puppetry and physical fabrication even as he leads VR exhibitions: live performance and material craft are his answer to what he calls the psychic assault of AI-generated imagery. His Buddhist sci-fi triptych at LACMA, *The Deer of Nine Colors*, is the current venue for these ideas made physical.

items.title: Neolithic people dragged 25-ton stones 11 miles across Yorkshire — isotopes now prove it
items.blurb: The Devil's Arrows — Britain's tallest standing stone alignment, largely ignored compared to Stonehenge — just got its origin story settled by isotopic analysis: the stones came from a quarry 18 kilometers away, moved by humans rather than glaciers. Each stone weighs around 25 tons. The researchers frame this not as engineering but as an "epic quest to create a sacred landscape" — which is worth sitting with: at some scale of effort, logistics becomes ritual.

facts.fact: The Devil's Arrows in Yorkshire are Britain's tallest standing stone alignment, yet they have received almost no scientific study compared to Stonehenge — the isotopic sourcing paper just published is among the first rigorous analyses of the site.

Houthi forces have now taken control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coastline including Perim Island at the mouth of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, meaning both of the global economy's two dominant maritime chokepoints face simultaneous active threat for the first time since World War II.

An EFF analysis found more than 6,300 Flock Safety license plate surveillance searches across 30+ agencies logged with the stated reason 'TBD', and one officer searched 19,000 cameras across 1,558 cities logging the reason as 'LMAO'.

The fugleramme bird frame project includes over 800 hand-curated illustration cutouts covering more than 400 species, every one taken from a real 19th-century natural history plate rather than generated by AI.

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink's confirmation that the US has 'on-orbit space control weapons' is the first time any senior US official has publicly stated that America has deployed weapons in orbit — ending decades of official silence on the subject.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film that operates like a generative system — memory, image, and time assembled into something that resembles consciousness more than narrative. Marker's footage from Japan and Guinea-Bissau becomes a meditation on how images encode culture and how culture encodes us; it will make you want to rebuild how you think about montage and meaning in your own work.

art_picks.title: All in the Present Must Be Transformed
art_picks.creator: William Kentridge
art_picks.why: Kentridge's practice is exactly the kind of obsessive system-as-art that hooks you: drawing, erasing, and filming the residue to make animation that embeds time into its own surface — the history of the mark is visible in every frame. His charcoal films are about politics, memory, and the body in ways that feel structural, not illustrative.

art_picks.title: Geogaddi
art_picks.creator: Boards of Canada
art_picks.why: A record engineered to feel like memory misremembering itself — built on decayed synthesis, off-kilter rhythms, and numerological obsession that the duo embedded into the structure of the album itself. The hidden system underneath the warm surface is exactly the kind of thing that makes you want to build something strange.

events.name: Iris van Herpen: Sculpting the Senses
events.why: 140+ haute couture pieces in dialogue with scientific artifacts, fossils, and natural history specimens — van Herpen's process uses biomimicry, fractal geometry, and neuroscience as design inputs, making this as much a systems exhibition as a fashion one, and the physical/digital boundary-blurring in her fabrication methods is genuinely relevant to your work.

events.name: Aziz Hazara: Coming Home / Cevdet Erek: Americas / Yining Fei: Feral Sediment — Opening Reception
events.why: Hazara's show returns material objects discarded at Bagram Airfield after the US military withdrawal — war as material culture, supply chain as monument — while Erek's sonic commission synchronizes with SculptureCenter's labyrinthine lower level; the triple opening makes this the sharpest single afternoon of the fall.

events.name: Johanna Hedva: Gravity, My / Favorite Enemy — Opening
events.venue: Center for Art, Research and Alliances (CARA), Manhattan
events.why: Hedva works at the edge where illness, myth, and political theory collapse into one another — their practice is exactly the kind of category-blurring (art as philosophy as ritual as community) that your taste signature describes, and CARA is a small enough space that you'll actually be in the room with the work.

events.name: Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony — Opening
events.why: The largest-ever survey of Jafa's four-decade practice, filling two floors of the newly expanded OMA-designed building — his montage logic borrows from jazz syncopation and Black visual archives in ways that rewire how you think about editing, rhythm, and what images actually do to people.

events.name: The Armory Show 2026
events.venue: Jacob K. Javits Convention Center, Manhattan
events.why: The 32nd edition features ~230 galleries from 30+ countries, with a curated Platform and Focus section centered on Caribbean and Caribbean-diaspora artists — worth one targeted afternoon for the gallery discovery alone, especially with everything else open this week.
